chunks: "A real-time operating system is an OS designed so that the timing of its behaviour is predictable.
Real-time doesn't mean fast; it means that tasks meet their deadlines reliably, because the worst-case response time is bounded and known.
The way it works is usually a preemptive, priority-based scheduler. Each task has a priority, and the scheduler always runs the highest-priority task that's ready.
If a more urgent task becomes ready, say because an interrupt gave it a semaphore, it preempts the current task straight away, after a context switch of a few microseconds.
Interrupt latency and the kernel's critical sections are kept short and bounded, and the primitives, like queues, mutexes and timers, have predictable behaviour.
There are different strictness levels. Hard real-time means a missed deadline is a failure, such as an airbag controller or a motor control loop.
Soft real-time means occasional misses just degrade quality, like dropped video frames. Examples are FreeRTOS, Zephyr, ThreadX, VxWorks and QNX.
A real-time OS doesn't guarantee that my system meets its deadlines.

I still need to assign priorities sensibly, bound execution times, avoid priority inversion with mutexes that support priority inheritance, and check schedulability, for example with rate-monotonic analysis or response-time calculations."
